title: Multi-Boundary Many-Body Quantum Teleportation
authors: Tal Schwartzman, Antonio F. Rotundo, Raz Monsonego, Shira Chapman
abstract: Unlike standard quantum teleportation, many-body teleportation uses scrambling to transmit quantum information. In this protocol, initially localized information spreads over many degrees of freedom and is later refocused at the receiver by a simple coupling between the systems, followed by further many-body evolution. The protocol was developed from models of traversable wormholes in holography and has become a useful probe of scrambling. In particular, it can distinguish genuine scrambling from decoherence or noise when out-of-time-order correlators fail, and can reveal signatures of different scrambling mechanisms, including the distinctive behavior expected in holographic systems. Holography predicts that related protocols can transmit information between selected boundaries of multi-boundary wormhole geometries. Motivated by this setting, we study single-qubit many-body teleportation among three systems of qubits. The initial state consists of EPR pairs distributed among them, providing a simple analogue of an infinite-temperature three-boundary holographic state. We analyze the protocol with one-dimensional and all-to-all dynamics, both analytically and numerically using random circuits. We find that the third system suppresses teleportation once the spreading message reaches the region of qubits that are entangled with it. In one dimension, both the minimum coupling required for successful teleportation and the fidelity depend on the distance from the injection site to this region, a feature reminiscent of holographic causal shadows. For all-to-all dynamics, successful teleportation is instead restricted to early times and to sufficiently few qubits entangled with the third system. A third system therefore provides spatial, or subsystem, resolution of information spreading that is absent from the two-sided protocol. Our results offer a step toward many-body teleportation networks.
summary: This work develops a multi-body quantum teleportation protocol using scrambling, motivated by holographic wormhole geometries. By extending the standard two-party setup to three parties, the authors demonstrate that the protocol can probe spatial information spreading, revealing features like holographic causal shadows. The results offer a new diagnostic tool for understanding information transfer in complex quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper generalizes quantum teleportation to a multi-body setting using quantum scrambling, drawing motivation from holographic models of traversable wormholes.
main_result: The three-party setup reveals spatial or subsystem resolution of information spreading, and the fidelity and required coupling exhibit dependencies on distance reminiscent of holographic causal shadows.
method: The analysis involves studying the protocol's success probability using both analytical techniques and numerical simulations employing random quantum circuits.
model_or_system: The system is a three-party quantum teleportation protocol involving three qubit systems (A, B, C), initialized with EPR pairs analogous to a three-boundary holographic state.
key_observables: Teleportation fidelity, minimum required coupling, and the dependence of these on distance from the injection site.
important_parameters: The dimensionality of dynamics (one-dimensional vs. all-to-all) and the number of parties (three).
main_assumptions: The analysis uses a single-qubit message and often relies on the infinite-temperature limit for holographic comparisons.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the two-sided protocol, the pair of pants geometry for the three-party state, and the causal structure including a causal shadow.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the standard two-party protocol to a three-party generalization, analyzing dynamics under 1D and all-to-all coupling, and comparing results to predictions from multi-boundary wormhole holography.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, testable quantum information protocol whose diagnostics (like spatial resolution) are directly linked to deep concepts in quantum gravity and holography, making it highly relevant for theoretical quantum information scientists.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A diagram of the two-sided protocol. The lines represent degrees of freedom, with the circuit evolving up- wards.
FIG. 2. The pair of pants geometry for the path integral representation of the wave function associated with the three-party generalization of the TFD state.

FIG. 3. Schematic representation of the t = 0 slice of a three-boundary wormhole. The dashed lines are the black hole horizons. In the boundary regions adjacent to the blue bulk regions, the entanglement is approximately bi- partite. The bulk region bounded by the red dashed lines is the causal shadow.

FIG. 4. The Penrose diagram of a black hole spacetime having a causal shadow with a particle that traverses it. This is a schematic representation of the causal structure of a section that contains two asymptotic regions in the three-boundary wormhole geometry [27]. The particle has a spacelike region to traverse that depends on the width of the causal shadow in this section. In the traversable wormhole protocol, the coupling induces negative averaged null energy and a corresponding null shift. This null shift should be large enough for the particle to cross the null- coordinate gap of the causal shadow.

FIG. 5. The operators spread with time, allowing for the peaked size mechanism to work. The regions to which the operators can spread without damaging the fidelity are limited in 1D by the distance to the sites that are entangled with C.
